newsitem.title: USA: Accounting board says issues new standard on EPS.
newsitem.headline: Accounting board says issues new standard on EPS.

text.p: The Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) said on Monday it issued a new standard for computing earnings per share (EPS).
The board also said it issued a new statement on capital structure.
The FASB said in a statement the new EPS standard was issued to simplify current U.S. standards for EPS and make them compatible with international standards.
It said the International Accounting Standards Committee (IASC) recently issued a comparable standard to the FASB's Statement 128 on EPS.
Statement 128 applies to entities with publicly held common stock and is effective for financial statements issued for periods ending after December 15, 1997.
"Statement 128 is the result of one of our first cooperative international standards-setting projects," FASB project manager Kim Petrone said.
"We are very pleased that we and the IASC were able to reach substantially identical conclusions."

The new standard replaces a previous guideline that required entities with simple capital structures to present a single "earnings per common share" on the face of the income statement, while those with complex structures had to present both "primary" and "fully diluted" EPS.
Petrone said the rules for computing primary EPS included "complicated and arbitrary provisions."
The new standard simplifies the proceess by replacing the presentation of primary EPS with a presentation of basic EPS.
The FASB also said it issued a new statement on capital structure to consolidate existing disclosure requirements for ease of retrieval.

The statement contains no change in disclosure requirements for companies subject to the previous requirements. It applies to all entities and is effective for financial statements issued for periods ending after December 15, 1997.
The FASB has no government authority, but is a private organization whose pronouncements on accounting are recognized as authoritative by the Securities and Exchange Commission.
